title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Result under Shared‑Generation Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) that tested whether deterministic verifier augmentation (generate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional repair) reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered intent→configuration tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Executed generation semantics used a single shared initial candidate per task (shared_initial_candidate) to conserve model calls, producing model_calls_used = 200 (preregistered independent per‑arm generation would have used ≈400). Observed (adversarial cluster): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0). Estimated paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Under these execution semantics the preregistered causal hypothesis was not testable because identical per‑pair generations removed the possible source of discordance. We publish the complete preregistered run and artifacts in the archived bundle, provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of the non‑informative outcome, and give concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration using the reserved exploratory cohort, and pilot checks) for informative repeats.

sections.introduction: LLM‑assisted translation of operator intent into device configuration promises productivity gains for Network Operations (NetOps), but unsafe or misordered changes can cause outages, security regressions, or policy violations. A widely recommended mitigation is tool‑augmentation: pairing LLM generators with deterministic validators or sandboxed simulators in a generate–validate–repair loop so that proposed changes are checked prior to execution. Prior work advocates such pipelines and presents prototype evidence that external verification can reduce explicit constraint violations on curated tasks, but conclusions depend strongly on evaluation semantics (how candidate generations are sampled, whether repairs are applied, and whether validation is sandboxed). To provide reproducible, inferentially principled evidence, we preregistered a paired experiment to measure the causal effect of adding a deterministic verifier to an LLM generation pipeline on the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe proposals under both benign and adversarial prompt clusters.
sections.related_work: Surveys and prototype reports document the rapid adoption of LLMs in NetOps tasks (intent translation, configuration synthesis, diagnosis, and limited remediation) and emphasize the need for careful safety evaluation and workflow‑centred benchmarks [1–3]. Experimental and methodological work has shown that tool‑augmentation (generate–validate–refine or divide–verify–refine) can reduce constraint violations when the external verifier faithfully encodes domain constraints; however, effect sizes are task‑dependent and sensitive to how candidates are sampled and scored [4–6]. Research on guardrails and schema‑based interfaces warns of operational trade‑offs: stricter validation can reduce unsafe acceptances but increase false refusals and operator workload unless ROC‑style diagnostics are reported and tested with adversarial templates [2,7]. Our study aligns with these lines by preregistering a paired estimand, using deterministic synthetic tasks and sandboxed validation, and archiving the full execution and analysis artifacts to support replayable failure analysis.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The experiment (cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1) specified a confirmatory paired binary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (guarded − baseline) on SAFE indicators returned by a deterministic sandbox validator. The planned confirmatory test was the exact two‑sided McNemar test with a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). The preregistration targeted N=200 tasks to detect an approximate 7 percentage‑point paired reduction with 80% power under an assumed baseline unsafe rate ≈10–15% and prespecified discordant proportions.

Task generation and scope. A deterministic task generator produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks constrained to single‑AS multi‑device topologies and limited fields (admin, mtu, vlan). Each task included initial_state, expected_final_state, and explicit workflow policies (required_sequence). Tasks were stratified into benign and adversarial clusters using a preregistered set of adversarial transforms; a reserved exploratory cohort (up to 50 tasks) was preregistered for calibration and ROC estimation.

Pipelines compared and generation semantics. Baseline: accept the LLM candidate and score post hoc with deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Guarded: validate the same candidate in a deterministic sandbox using deterministic_netops_validator_v5; repairs were permitted by design but were not invoked in the confirmatory episodes. The preregistration allowed two generation semantics: (A) independent per‑arm generation (one LLM call per arm per task) or (B) shared_initial_candidate (one shared LLM call per task scored by both arms). To conserve hosted model budget the executed run used the shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false), resulting in a single LLM call per task shared across arms.

Scoring and analysis. The deterministic validator applied full_intent_constraint_validation and emitted a deterministic valid flag plus structured violation lists; confirmatory binary outcomes equaled validator.valid (1 = SAFE, 0 = UNSAFE). Paired analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1 to compute the 2×2 contingency (n11, n10, n01, n00), exact McNemar p‑value, and paired bootstrap CI. Missingness rules and retry policies from the preregistration were enforced deterministically.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The confirmed execution completed 400 episodes (200 paired episodes) with model_calls_used = 200 (shared_initial_candidate semantics) and no technical failures or exclusions. Provider audit confirmed hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and no cross‑condition cache reuse. The reserved exploratory cohort was not consumed prior to confirmatory execution.

Primary contingency and inferential outputs. The deterministic validator labeled every confirmatory candidate SAFE: baseline SAFE = 200/200 and guarded SAFE = 200/200. The paired contingency is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. From these counts the paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (resamples = 10000; seed = 1729) is degenerate at [0.0, 0.0]. These numerical artifacts are identical to the archived analysis summaries.

Representative traces and repairs. Representative scoring records show that the raw generated candidate was identical for baseline and guarded episodes and that validator.validation_before/after reported violation_count = 0 and valid = true in every examined case. repair_provider_trace fields are null for all confirmatory episodes, confirming that no automatic repairs were applied and that guarded outcomes reflect pure validation rather than repaired candidates.

Missingness and contamination. The analysis recorded complete_pairs = 200 with zero failed or unscorable episodes and no contamination flags. The absence of discordant pairs persisted across the entire confirmatory set.
sections.discussion:
Why the confirmatory contrast was untestable. The paired design tests differences by observing discordant outcomes between arms. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the only mechanisms that could create discordance were: (i) arm‑specific stochastic generation (disabled by sharing), (ii) deterministic repairs invoked in the guarded arm (none occurred), or (iii) nondeterministic validator behaviour (no nondeterminism observed). The conjunction of a shared candidate per pair, a validator that labeled all sampled candidates SAFE, and absent repairs produced a ceiling contingency (n11=200), which mechanically prevents McNemar‑style inference.

Implications for preregistered design and power. The preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline unsafe rate and sufficient discordance; those assumptions failed here. The modeled resource arithmetic is explicit: independent per‑arm generation would have required ≈400 model calls whereas the executed shared semantics used 200 calls. When budgets force shared draws, the estimand must change (see next paragraph) or the reserve exploratory cohort must be consumed to calibrate adversarial transforms prior to confirmatory execution.

Recommendations for informative repeats (artifact‑grounded). (1) Use independent per‑arm generation for paired causal contrasts unless the guarded arm reliably performs deterministic candidate repairs; budget accordingly (≈2× model calls). (2) Prior to confirmatory execution, consume the preregistered exploratory reserve to tune adversarial transforms until the baseline unsafe rate aligns with power assumptions; fix calibration parameters before committing to confirmatory trials. (3) Instrument and archive repair traces when repairs are enabled and report UNSAFE→SAFE conversion rates and any repair‑introduced violations. (4) Add a deterministic pilot check: run a small holdout and inspect contingency counts; if the pilot yields no discordant pairs, follow preregistered contingency‑preserving adaptation paths (e.g., enable independent per‑arm draws) rather than proceeding to an uninformative confirmatory test.

Alternative estimands when independent draws are infeasible. If model‑call budgets preclude independent draws, consider estimands that remain testable under shared semantics: (a) estimate the absolute unsafe‑proposal rate of the LLM baseline with CIs; (b) treat the guarded pipeline as an accept/reject gate and report refusal and post‑repair SAFE rates (requires repairs); or (c) reserve exploratory ROC estimation to quantify verifier trade‑offs. These alternatives preserve inferential validity but shift resource and preregistration requirements.

Threats to validity and externality. The study used synthetic single‑AS tasks limited to a small configuration field set and evaluated a single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) with a deterministic sandbox validator. Zero unsafe detections here do not imply production readiness: validator completeness, multi‑vendor interactions, cross‑AS policies, and human‑operator workflows remain outside this experiment’s scope. The archived artifacts allow replay and targeted extension but cannot substitute for field validation.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived preregistered paired experiment comparing gpt‑5‑mini baseline generation and a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; McNemar p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]). Because identical per‑pair generations were used and no repairs were applied, the preregistered causal hypothesis was untestable in this run. The substantive contribution is methodological and reproducibility‑centred: a complete deterministic preregistered run with archived artifacts that permit deterministic replay; an artifact‑grounded diagnosis explaining why the execution was non‑informative for verifier efficacy; and concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration via the exploratory reserve, pilot checks, and repair instrumentation) for informative repeats. Researchers and operators planning confirmatory paired contrasts should ensure that generation semantics and budgeting align with the estimand to avoid mechanically untestable outcomes.

Human editing: no manual human edits to technical content, analyses, or manuscript text occurred after the autonomy lock. limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases or explicit injected unsafe examples are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in synthetic sandboxed states; external validation of validator completeness against real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
